description:
Mia Bennett has always been good at planning everything except the things that truly matter. When an unexpected opportunity takes her on a journey through unfamiliar cities, quiet villages, and roads she never intended to follow, she begins to discover that traveling is not always about finding new places. Sometimes, it is about seeing yourself differently once you finally leave the familiar behind.

Along the way, Mia meets people who change the way she sees the world, experiences moments she could never have planned, and slowly learns that some journeys are not meant to lead us back to who we were. They are meant to show us who we might become.

chapters.title: The Ticket on the Table
chapters.content:
Mia Bennett had spent most of her adult life helping other people leave.

Every morning, she arrived at the travel agency a little before nine, unlocked the glass door, turned on the lights, and watched the first sunlight of the day spread across the posters covering the walls. There were photographs of places she had never visited everywhere she looked: turquoise water beneath white cliffs, narrow streets filled with flowers, mountains disappearing into clouds, old European squares crowded with cafés and bicycles, and beaches where the sand seemed almost impossibly white. The pictures were beautiful enough to make people stop in the window, and every now and then Mia would catch someone standing outside, studying one of them with the same expression she had seen on hundreds of customers over the years. Curiosity first. Then longing. Then calculation. How much would it cost? How many days could they take off? Who would they go with? Could they really afford to leave?

Mia knew how to answer almost all of those questions.

She knew which airlines had the best connections, which hotels were worth their prices, which train stations were easier to navigate, which cities became crowded during certain months, and which beaches looked wonderful in photographs but were disappointing in person. She could build a ten-day itinerary in less than an hour, find a cheaper alternative without making it feel cheap, and tell from a customer's questions whether they wanted adventure or simply a comfortable version of somewhere unfamiliar. She knew how to reassure nervous travelers and how to explain that missing a train in another country was not necessarily the disaster they imagined it would be.

What she did not know was what it felt like to be the person buying the ticket.

She had been working at the agency for almost six years.

In that time, she had helped honeymooners choose hotels in Santorini, families organize road trips across the country, couples plan anniversary weekends, and groups of friends arrange complicated journeys involving three countries and seven different trains. She had booked flights for people who had never been on an airplane before and helped experienced travelers find places they had never heard of.

Mia had traveled, technically.

She had taken weekend trips with her parents when she was younger. She had spent a few summers visiting relatives. She had gone away with friends during university, although those trips had usually been more about late nights and cheap food than about seeing anything properly.

But since starting her career, she had stayed close to home.

There was always a reason.

Work was busy.

Her apartment needed something.

Her mother had needed help.

Sophie had been moving.

The timing wasn't right.

She would travel eventually.

Eventually had become a surprisingly comfortable word.

It allowed Mia to imagine a future version of herself who was more spontaneous, more confident, more willing to spend money on experiences instead of practical things. That future Mia would wake up one morning and decide to buy a ticket somewhere she had never been. She would pack a small suitcase, leave her apartment, and feel completely certain that she was doing the right thing.

The current Mia simply hadn't become that person yet.

On Thursday morning, she was sitting behind the agency's front desk when her coworker Daniel dropped a folder onto the counter.

"Family of five," he said. "They want to do Italy in twelve days."

Mia looked at the folder.

"Five people?"

"Two adults, three children."

"How old?"

"Eight, eleven, and thirteen."

Mia opened the file.

"Then they're going to hate twelve days in Italy."

Daniel laughed.

"That's what I said."

"They'll be exhausted by day four."

"Exactly."

She turned the folder toward herself and began reading the notes.

"Where do they want to go?"

"Rome, Florence, Venice, and the Amalfi Coast."

Mia looked up.

"Of course."

"What?"

"Nothing."

Daniel pulled a chair over.

"You've been doing this too long."

"I know."

"You can tell what people are going to do before they tell you."

Mia smiled.

"That's because everyone wants to see everything."

"And you?"

She looked at him.

"What about me?"

"If you had twelve days and unlimited money, where would you go?"

Mia opened her mouth.

Then stopped.

She looked at the photographs on the wall.

There were hundreds of possibilities.

For a few seconds, she imagined herself somewhere far away. She imagined walking through an unfamiliar city early in the morning, before the streets became crowded. She imagined sitting in a café where she couldn't understand every conversation around her. She imagined looking at a train timetable and realizing she had no idea where one of the destinations was.

Then the image disappeared.

"I don't know," she said.

Daniel stared at her.

"You work at a travel agency."

"I know."

"You really don't have an answer?"

Mia smiled.

"I plan other people's trips. That's different."

"How?"

"Other people have somewhere they want to go."

Daniel leaned back in his chair.

"That's a little depressing."

"Maybe."

He laughed and returned to his desk.

Mia looked at the family itinerary again.

She began making changes.

The Amalfi Coast would be too complicated with the children. She suggested reducing the number of cities and adding more time in Florence. She found a quieter hotel near the train station in Rome and changed one of the connections so they wouldn't have to wake up before six.

She was good at this.

That had never been the problem.

The problem was that she was beginning to wonder why she was so good at arranging lives she wasn't living.

At lunch, she walked to the café across the street with her friend Claire.

Claire had worked at the agency for almost as long as Mia had, although they had become friends only in the last two years. She was the kind of person who could order something different from the menu every time she visited a restaurant, even when she already knew what she liked.

Mia always ordered the same thing.

"You've been quiet," Claire said.

"I'm thinking."

"That's dangerous."

"Apparently everyone thinks I'm dangerous when I think."

Claire smiled.

They sat near the window.

Outside, the city moved through its usual afternoon rhythm. Buses stopped at the corner. People crossed the street carrying shopping bags. A delivery driver hurried into a building with a stack of boxes balanced against his chest.

Claire stirred her coffee.

"Are you still thinking about taking some time off?"

Mia looked at her.

"When did I say that?"

"Last month."

"I don't remember."

"I do."

Mia smiled.

"I said maybe."

"You've been saying maybe for six months."

"Have I?"

"Yes."

Mia looked down at her plate.

"Maybe I don't know where I'd go."

"You work at a travel agency."

"That doesn't mean I know where I want to go."

Claire leaned back.

"Then go somewhere you don't want to go."

Mia laughed.

"That makes no sense."

"It does."

"No, it really doesn't."

"Everyone travels to the places they think they're supposed to want. Paris. Rome. New York. Bali. Whatever is on everyone's list. Maybe you should go somewhere you know nothing about."

Mia considered it.

"That sounds expensive."

"Everything sounds expensive when you're thinking about it from your desk."

Mia looked at her.

Claire smiled.

"Take a trip."

"I can't just take a trip."

"Why not?"

Mia opened her mouth.

She had several answers.

Because she had work.

Because she had responsibilities.

Because she had plans.

Because she was saving money.

Because she didn't know anyone there.

Because she didn't like traveling alone.

Because it would be easier next year.

Instead, she said, "I don't know."

Claire pointed at her.

"That's the first honest answer you've given me."

Mia laughed.

The conversation moved to other things.

A difficult customer.

A new restaurant Claire wanted to try.

A movie they had both forgotten to watch.

By the time they returned to work, the idea had almost disappeared from Mia's mind.

Almost.

That evening, she stopped at the supermarket on the way home.

She bought bread, fruit, pasta, coffee, and the same yogurt she always bought. She stood in the checkout line looking at a magazine with a photograph of a mountain village on the cover.

The headline read:

TEN PLACES TO VISIT BEFORE YOU TURN THIRTY.

Mia stared at it.

She was twenty-eight.

She had two years.

She almost laughed.

The magazine went back on the shelf.

When she arrived home, she changed clothes, made pasta, and ate dinner while watching television.

Her apartment was small but comfortable. Everything had its place. Books were arranged by height on the shelf. Shoes were lined up near the door. The kitchen counters were almost always clean.

Mia liked order.

Order made things easier.

After dinner, she washed the dishes and opened her laptop.

She had planned to answer a few work emails.

Instead, she found herself looking at flights.

She didn't search for anywhere specific.

She simply entered a date two months away.

Then she stared at the map.

Europe.

North Africa.

South America.

Asia.

The world looked enormous on a computer screen.

She clicked on a city at random.

Then another.

She read about trains, hotels, museums, restaurants, walking tours.

She imagined herself there.

The feeling was exciting for approximately seven minutes.

Then she closed the laptop.

"Maybe next year," she said.

It was easier that way.

On Friday morning, Mia arrived at work to find an envelope waiting on her desk.

Her name was written across the front.

She recognized the handwriting immediately.

Claire.

Mia opened it.

Inside was a folded piece of paper.

I know you won't do it if I only tell you to. So I'm giving you a reason.

Mia frowned.

There was something else inside.

A plane ticket.

She unfolded it slowly.

Her eyes moved across the details.

Her heart stopped.

It was a flight to Portugal.

Departure in ten days.

Return three weeks later.

Mia stared at the ticket.

Claire appeared beside her.

"Before you say anything, listen."

Mia looked up.

"What is this?"

"My sister was supposed to go."

"To Portugal?"

"Yes."

"When?"

"Next week."

"Why isn't she going?"

"She got accepted into a program in another city. She leaves sooner than expected."

Mia looked back at the ticket.

"And you?"

"I can't go."

"Why?"

"Work."

Mia raised an eyebrow.

"You just gave me a plane ticket."

"I know."

"You're telling me to travel while you're staying here?"

"Yes."

"That's ridiculous."

"Probably."

Claire pulled up a chair.

"My sister said she couldn't get a refund. I told her I'd figure something out. Then I thought about you."

Mia stared at her.

"Why me?"

Claire looked at her for a moment.

"Because you keep talking about traveling like you're waiting for permission."

Mia didn't answer.

Claire continued.

"You know everything about how to get somewhere. You know how to find hotels, trains, flights, restaurants. You know which neighborhoods are safe and which museums need reservations. But you don't actually go anywhere."

Mia looked down at the ticket.

"I can't just leave for three weeks."

"Why not?"

"I have work."

"Your vacation days."

"My apartment."

"Will still be there."

"My parents."

"Will survive."

"My routines."

Claire smiled.

"Those might actually be the problem."

Mia laughed nervously.

"This is crazy."

"Probably."

"I've never traveled alone."

"I know."

"I don't even know if I want to."

"I know."

Mia looked at the ticket again.

Portugal.

Ten days.

Three weeks.

The words seemed impossible.

"What if I don't go?"

"Then you don't go."

"That's it?"

"That's it."

Claire stood.

"I didn't give it to you because I want you to go. I gave it to you because I want you to have the choice."

Mia watched her walk away.

For the rest of the morning, the ticket remained on her desk.

She tried to work.

She answered emails.

She changed hotel reservations.

She called an airline about a passenger's missed connection.

She helped a couple choose between two hotels in Lisbon.

The entire time, the ticket sat beside her keyboard.

At one point, Daniel walked past.

He stopped.

"What's that?"

Mia covered it with her hand.

"Nothing."

He looked at her.

"That is clearly not nothing."

She hesitated.

Then she showed him.

He read the details.

"Portugal?"

"Apparently."

"You're going?"

"I don't know."

He looked at her.

"Why not?"

Mia laughed.

"Because it's a plane ticket."

"Yes."

"To another country."

"That's generally where international plane tickets go."

She smiled.

"I've never traveled alone."

Daniel looked at the ticket again.

"Maybe that's why you should."

Mia frowned.

"Everyone is suddenly very confident about my life."

He smiled.

"I'm not telling you what to do."

"Then what are you saying?"

Daniel looked toward the window.

"I'm saying that sometimes the hardest part of a journey is deciding that you're allowed to take it."

Mia looked at him.

He returned to his desk.

She looked at the ticket again.

That afternoon, she called her mother.

"Mom?"

"Hi, sweetheart."

"Can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

Mia hesitated.

"I'm thinking about taking a trip."

There was a pause.

"Where?"

"Portugal."

Another pause.

"With who?"

"Alone."

Her mother was quiet for long enough that Mia could imagine every possible concern forming in her head.

"How long?"

"Three weeks."

"Mia."

"I know."

"You've never gone anywhere alone."

"I know."

"Do you know anyone there?"

"No."

Her mother sighed.

"Then why do you want to go?"

Mia looked through the office window.

She thought about all the answers she could give.

Because Claire gave her a ticket.

Because she needed a break.

Because she had vacation days.

Because Portugal was beautiful.

Because she had always wanted to travel.

But none of those answers felt completely true.

"I think," she said slowly, "I want to know what it feels like to go somewhere without already knowing exactly what I'm going to do."

Her mother was quiet.

Then she said, "That sounds like you."

Mia smiled.

"What does that mean?"

"You've always been curious. You just don't usually let yourself follow it."

Mia looked down.

"Are you worried?"

"Of course."

"Should I go?"

Her mother laughed softly.

"That's not my decision."

Mia smiled.

"I know."

"You should make the decision because you want to make it, not because someone else tells you to."

Mia leaned back in her chair.

"Okay."

"Call me when you arrive."

"I will."

"Every day."

"Mom."

"Every other day."

Mia laughed.

"Deal."

When she hung up, she looked at the ticket again.

For the first time, she didn't put it away.

She took it home that evening.

She placed it on the kitchen table.

Then she made dinner.

Afterward, she washed the dishes.

She took a shower.

She changed into pajamas.

She watched half an episode of a show she wasn't really following.

The ticket remained on the table.

At eleven thirty, Mia stood in the kitchen.

She looked at it.

Ten days.

She could still say no.

She could give it back to Claire.

She could explain that it wasn't the right time.

She could return to her routine.

Nothing would be lost.

That was the strange part.

Saying no would be easy.

Nothing would change.

Mia picked up the ticket.

She looked at the name printed beneath the flight details.

Mia Bennett.

For some reason, seeing her own name there made everything feel more real.

She walked to her bedroom.

Then she stopped.

She returned to the kitchen.

She opened her laptop.

She searched for Portugal.

Lisbon.

Porto.

Small towns.

Train routes.

Coastal roads.

She looked at photographs until midnight.

At twelve fifteen, she opened the airline website.

She entered her booking reference.

The reservation appeared on the screen.

Manage your trip.

Her finger hovered over the trackpad.

There was an option to cancel.

Mia stared at it.

Then she closed the page.

She opened a new document.

At the top, she typed:

PORTUGAL

Underneath, she wrote:

Things I want to see.

She stopped.

Then deleted the sentence.

She wrote:

Things I don't want to miss.

That felt better.

She added the first item.

Walk somewhere without knowing where I'm going.

Then another.

Eat something I can't pronounce.

Another.

Take a train without checking every detail first.

Mia smiled.

She kept writing.

When she finally looked at the clock, it was nearly one in the morning.

The list wasn't long.

It didn't need to be.

She closed the laptop.

The ticket was still on the table.

Mia picked it up and carried it to her bedroom.

She placed it beside her bed.

For a long moment, she stood there looking at it.

Then she turned off the light.

She didn't know exactly what would happen in ten days.

She didn't know what the streets would look like, whether she would feel lonely, whether she would regret going, or whether three weeks would be enough to change anything at all.

She only knew that, for the first time in a very long time, tomorrow wasn't simply another day waiting for her.

It was the beginning of somewhere else.

And somewhere between the fear of leaving and the possibility of discovering what waited beyond the familiar, Mia realized that perhaps the most important journeys did not begin when you reached the airport.

They began much earlier.

They began the moment you stopped telling yourself that you could go someday.

chapters.title: The First Morning Somewhere Else
chapters.content:
The first thing Mia noticed about Lisbon was that it sounded different.

Not dramatically different. There were no bells announcing her arrival, no sudden feeling that she had stepped into another version of the world. It was simply the sound of voices around her that she could not always understand, the unfamiliar rhythm of announcements at the airport, the wheels of suitcases rolling across polished floors, and the occasional Portuguese word that sounded familiar enough to recognize and strange enough to remind her that she was somewhere else.

She had been awake for almost twenty hours.

Her flight had left late the previous evening, and although she had managed to sleep for a few hours, it had been the kind of sleep that came in fragments. She had watched the lights of the city disappear beneath the airplane, closed her eyes, opened them again, checked the time, looked out at the darkness beyond the window, and eventually slept just long enough to wake up feeling as though she had forgotten what day it was.

Now she stood in the airport arrivals hall with one suitcase, one backpack, and a piece of paper containing the address of her hotel.

She looked at the paper.

Then at the signs.

Then back at the paper.

For someone who worked at a travel agency, Mia felt remarkably unprepared.

She had planned the trip. She had checked the airport layout. She had downloaded maps. She had saved the hotel address offline. She had even taken screenshots of the train connections she might need.

And yet, standing there with her suitcase beside her, she suddenly understood the difference between knowing how a journey worked and actually being inside it.

She was alone.

There was no Claire beside her. No mother asking whether she had eaten. No coworker telling her which train to take. No familiar street waiting outside.

Just Lisbon.

Mia took a breath.

"Okay," she whispered.

She pulled her suitcase behind her and walked toward the exit.

The morning air was warmer than she had expected.

Outside the airport, taxis waited in a long line, buses moved slowly along the road, and people stood around checking phones and luggage. Mia stopped for a moment just to look.

She had seen photographs of Lisbon hundreds of times. She had recommended hotels there. She had helped customers choose neighborhoods. She had explained how long it took to get from the airport to the city center.

None of that had prepared her for the first sensation of actually being there.

The sunlight felt different. The air smelled different. Even the buildings in the distance seemed unfamiliar in a way that photographs could never capture.

Mia found the transportation area and followed the signs toward the metro.

Her first train was easy.

The second was less easy.

At one point, she stood on the platform staring at a map and realized she had been looking at the wrong line for nearly five minutes.

A man standing nearby noticed.

He pointed toward another platform.

"That one."

Mia looked at him.

"Thank you."

He smiled and walked away.

She followed the direction he had indicated.

When she finally arrived near her hotel, she was tired enough that she briefly considered going straight to bed.

The hotel was a small place on a quiet street, with pale walls, narrow balconies, and a reception desk that looked as though it had been there for decades. The woman behind the desk welcomed her warmly, checked her reservation, and handed her a key.

"Your room is on the third floor."

Mia thanked her.

Then she asked the question she had been holding since the airport.

"Is there somewhere nearby where I can get breakfast?"

The woman smiled.

"Of course."

She pointed toward the street.

"Go left, then right at the church. You will see a little café."

Mia nodded.

"Thank you."

"You are welcome."

She took her suitcase upstairs.

Her room was smaller than the photographs had suggested, but Mia didn't mind.

There was a narrow bed, a wooden desk, a small wardrobe, and a window overlooking the street.

She put her suitcase beside the bed.

Then she sat down.

She should have unpacked.

Instead, she stared at the ceiling.

Her body wanted sleep.

Her mind wanted to understand where she was.

She had imagined this moment many times during the ten days before the trip. She had imagined opening the hotel window and feeling excited. She had imagined walking into the city with her camera. She had imagined calling Claire and saying, "I did it."

She had not imagined being so tired that she wasn't sure whether she wanted to cry or laugh.

Mia reached for her phone.

There was a message from her mother.

"Mom: Did you arrive safely?"

Mia smiled.

She typed back.

"Mia: Yes. I'm at the hotel."

Three dots appeared almost immediately.

"Mom: Did you eat?"

Mia laughed.

"Mia: Not yet."

"Mom: Eat."

"Mia: Yes, Mom."

She put the phone away.

Then she stood.

If she slept now, she knew what would happen. She would wake up in the afternoon, feel disoriented, and spend the rest of the day inside the hotel trying to convince herself that she wasn't wasting time.

She had not come all this way to hide in a room.

So she left.

The street outside was quiet.

Mia followed the directions the hotel receptionist had given her, turning left at the corner and then right when she saw the church.

She expected to find the café immediately.

Instead, she walked past it.

Then she realized her mistake and turned around.

It was almost embarrassingly small.

A narrow doorway. Three tables outside. A blue sign above the entrance.

She stepped inside.

The café was warm and bright, with shelves filled with jars and packages behind the counter. The smell of coffee and freshly baked bread filled the room.

A woman stood behind the counter.

She looked to be in her sixties, perhaps a little older, with short silver hair and a red scarf around her neck.

She smiled at Mia.

"Good morning."

Mia smiled back.

"Good morning."

The woman waited.

Mia looked at the menu.

Most of it was in Portuguese.

She recognized enough to understand that there was coffee, bread, pastries, eggs, and several things she could not identify.

She pointed at one.

"What is that?"

The woman leaned forward.

"Pastel de nata."

Mia nodded as if she understood completely.

"And what is it?"

The woman laughed.

"Try."

Mia smiled.

"Okay."

She ordered coffee and one pastel de nata.

The woman placed the pastry on a small plate and slid it toward her.

Mia took a bite.

Her expression changed immediately.

The woman laughed.

"Good?"

"Very good."

"First time?"

Mia nodded.

"First morning."

The woman studied her.

"You are alone."

It wasn't a question.

"Yes."

"Vacation?"

"Yes."

"From where?"

Mia told her.

The woman nodded.

"And why Portugal?"

Mia hesitated.

She had answered that question several times before leaving.

Because she had always wanted to visit. Because Claire's sister couldn't go. Because the ticket had been available. Because she needed a break.

None of those answers seemed right in that moment.

"I don't know," she said.

The woman smiled.

"Good."

Mia laughed.

"Good?"

"People who know exactly why they come usually have too many plans."

She picked up a cup and began cleaning it.

"What is your name?"

"Mia."

The woman nodded.

"I'm Teresa."

Mia looked around the café.

"Do you own this place?"

"Yes."

"How long?"

"Twenty-three years."

Mia looked surprised.

"Twenty-three?"

Teresa smiled.

"Long time."

"What made you stay?"

Teresa placed the cup on a shelf.

"Stay where?"

"Here."

Teresa looked at the café. Then through the window. Then back at Mia.

"I don't think I stayed."

Mia frowned.

"What do you mean?"

"I changed."

Mia waited.

Teresa smiled.

"The place stayed. I changed inside it."

Mia looked down at her coffee.

It was a strange answer.

But somehow it stayed with her.

She finished breakfast slowly.

Before leaving, she asked Teresa if there was somewhere nearby she should visit.

Teresa pointed toward the door.

"Walk."

"Where?"

"Anywhere."

Mia laughed.

"That's not very specific."

"It doesn't need to be."

Teresa took a napkin and drew a rough map.

"Go toward the river. Don't use your phone."

Mia looked at the drawing.

"Don't use my phone?"

"Not yet."

"Why?"

Teresa smiled.

"If you know where you are going, you will only see what you expected."

Mia folded the napkin.

"That's a little dangerous."

"Only if you are in a hurry."

Mia thanked her and left.

Outside, the city had become busier.

She took her phone from her pocket.

Then she remembered Teresa.

She put it away.

For the first few minutes, she felt ridiculous.

She had no idea where she was going.

She passed a bakery, a small grocery store, a flower shop, and a narrow building covered in blue and white tiles.

She turned down a street simply because she liked the way it looked.

The street became narrower. Then steeper.

Mia laughed when she realized she had underestimated the hills.

She stopped halfway up, breathing heavily.

A man walking past smiled.

"First day?"

Mia nodded.

He laughed.

"Good luck."

She continued.

At the top, she found a small square.

There were two benches, several trees, and a view between the buildings that opened toward the river.

Mia stopped.

She had not planned to come there.

No travel guide had told her to stop there.

No customer had ever mentioned it.

There was nothing particularly famous about it.

But she liked it.

She sat on a bench.

For the first time since leaving home, she felt completely still.

People moved around her.

A child chased a pigeon. An old man read a newspaper. Two women talked quietly on another bench. A delivery driver carried boxes into a nearby shop.

The city continued without paying attention to her.

Mia liked that too.

She took out her notebook.

She had bought it specifically for the trip.

On the first page, she had written the date.

Below it, she had written:

"Portugal — Day One."

She looked at the empty page.

Then she wrote:

"I thought traveling would feel bigger."

She paused.

Then continued.

"It doesn't."

She looked at the sentence.

After a moment, she added:

"Maybe that's the point."

She closed the notebook.

Her phone vibrated.

A message from Claire.

"Claire: Are you alive?"

Mia smiled.

"Mia: Yes."

"Claire: Do you hate me?"

"Mia: Not yet."

"Claire: Where are you?"

Mia looked around.

She had no idea.

She laughed.

"Mia: I don't know."

There was a long pause.

Then:

"Claire: You are finally traveling."

Mia smiled.

She put the phone away.

The rest of the morning passed without a plan.

She walked downhill. She found a small market and bought fruit she didn't recognize. She entered a shop selling postcards and spent ten minutes choosing one she would probably never send. She stopped at another café and listened to two people having a conversation she couldn't understand.

At some point, she realized she had been walking for almost three hours.

Her feet hurt.

She was hungry again.

She was also happier than she had expected.

When she finally returned to the hotel, she sat on the edge of the bed and looked at her suitcase.

She hadn't unpacked. She hadn't followed her itinerary. She hadn't visited a single major attraction. She hadn't taken the photograph she had imagined taking.

And yet, when she thought about the morning, she couldn't think of anything she would change.

She opened her notebook again.

This time, she wrote more.

"I met Teresa."

"I ate something I couldn't pronounce."

"I walked somewhere without knowing where I was going."

"I got lost."

She stopped.

Then added:

"I wasn't afraid."

Mia read the sentence several times.

She realized it wasn't completely true.

She had been afraid.

She had simply kept walking anyway.

That afternoon, she finally unpacked.

She placed her clothes in the wardrobe, put her shoes near the door, and organized the small things she had brought with her.

The familiar routine made her feel calmer.

But when she finished, she did something she would never have done at home.

She left her suitcase half-open.

She didn't need everything to be perfectly organized.

Not today.

She sat by the window and watched the street.

A woman carried groceries home. A couple walked past holding hands. A boy rode a bicycle too quickly and nearly fell before laughing. A dog barked from a balcony.

The city was full of ordinary moments.

Mia had come expecting something extraordinary.

Instead, she had found a morning.

And somehow, that seemed like enough.

That evening, she went downstairs to ask the receptionist about dinner.

Before she could speak, the woman smiled.

"Did you walk?"

Mia nodded.

"All morning."

"Good."

Mia smiled.

"I got lost."

The woman shrugged.

"That is sometimes the best way."

Mia thought of Teresa.

Perhaps everyone in this city had decided that getting lost was useful.

She stepped outside again.

The evening air was cooler.

She didn't check the map.

She simply chose a direction and started walking.

For the first time in years, Mia had no idea what the next hour would look like.

And instead of making her uncomfortable, the uncertainty felt strangely close to freedom.

chapters.title: The Road That Wasn't on the Map
chapters.content:
Mia had planned to leave Lisbon on Wednesday morning. The plan was simple. She would wake early, have breakfast at the hotel, take the train north, and arrive in a small village before lunch. She had chosen the village because it was far enough from the city to feel different but close enough that she wouldn't spend an entire day traveling. There was a small guesthouse overlooking the hills, a market on Saturdays, a church built several centuries ago, and a walking trail that led toward the edge of a forest.

She had booked the room three weeks earlier. She had printed the reservation. She had saved the train times. She had even marked the station entrance on her phone.

At seven forty-five that morning, Mia was standing on the platform when an announcement came over the speakers. She understood almost none of it. People around her began moving. Some looked at their phones. Others spoke to one another. A man hurried toward the information desk.

Mia checked the departure board. Her train was no longer listed. She stared at the screen, then refreshed the information on her phone. Still nothing.

A few minutes later, she finally understood what had happened. The train had been canceled.

Mia stood still for a moment. She had spent years believing that being prepared meant being protected from surprises. She had built entire routines around that idea. If she checked enough details, left early enough, organized carefully enough, she could avoid the unpleasantness of uncertainty.

Now she was standing in a foreign train station with a suitcase beside her, looking at a canceled train. There was nothing to organize. Nothing to prevent. It had simply happened.

Mia walked toward the information desk. The line was already long. She joined it.

Twenty minutes later, she reached the front and explained where she needed to go. The employee spoke quickly. Mia understood the words "bus," "another station," and "two hours." She looked confused. The employee repeated the explanation more slowly, then pointed toward a printed schedule.

Mia thanked him. She walked away and found a bench.

Two hours.

She could wait. She could also give up. The hotel in the village was non-refundable, but that wasn't the real problem. She had planned the day so carefully that the thought of abandoning it made her strangely upset.

She looked at the station around her. People were coming and going. A child was eating a pastry while sitting on a suitcase. A woman was talking on the phone. A young couple was studying a map.

And then she noticed a man sitting several seats away. He had a camera hanging from his shoulder and a backpack resting beside his feet. He was looking at the canceled train notice on his phone.

He looked up. Their eyes met. He smiled politely. Mia smiled back. Then he looked at the schedule again.

A few minutes passed. Finally, he turned toward her.

"You're going to Vale do Sol?"

Mia looked surprised. "Yes."

He pointed at the paper in her hand. "I saw the address."

She looked down. The name of the village was printed at the top.

"You too?"

He nodded. "Apparently."

Mia laughed. "Apparently?"

"Apparently we're not going there by train."

She smiled. "I was beginning to suspect that."

He stood and picked up his backpack. "I'm Lucas."

"Mia."

"First time?"

She nodded. "Yours?"

"Not the village." He looked toward the platform. "But I haven't been there in years."

Mia glanced at his camera. "Are you a photographer?"

"Sometimes."

"What does that mean?"

He smiled. "It means I take photographs when I don't know what else to do."

Mia laughed. "That's an unusual profession."

"I'm not sure it's a profession."

They stood together near the schedule. Lucas pointed at a line.

"There is a regional bus from the next station."

"How do we get there?"

"That's the interesting part."

Mia looked at him.

He smiled. "We walk."

She checked her phone. The next connection was in just under an hour. They had enough time.

Mia hesitated. Walking through an unfamiliar city with a stranger was not something she would normally consider. Then again, almost nothing about the last few days had been something she normally considered.

"Okay," she said.

Lucas picked up his backpack. "Okay."

They left the station together. The morning was warm, and the streets were already beginning to fill. Mia walked beside him, pulling her suitcase behind her.

For the first few minutes, they didn't say much. Then Lucas asked, "Why are you going to Vale do Sol?"

Mia thought about it. "Because I booked a room there."

He laughed. "That's very practical."

"What about you?"

"I have a friend who told me I should go."

"That's it?"

"Pretty much."

Mia looked at him. "You're not very good at explaining things."

"I've been told."

They turned onto a quieter street.

Mia noticed the camera again. "Are you traveling for work?"

"No."

"Vacation?"

"Maybe."

She laughed. "Maybe?"

Lucas looked at her. "You ask a lot of questions."

"You started."

"Fair."

They walked for another block. Then Lucas said, "I'm taking photographs for a project."

"What kind?"

"Places people are leaving."

Mia slowed slightly. "Leaving?"

"Old houses. Small businesses. Villages. Things that are disappearing."

She looked around. "Why?"

"I don't know yet."

Mia smiled. "Everyone says they don't know things here."

Lucas laughed. "Maybe that's because we're traveling."

They reached the next station. The bus was already waiting.

Mia checked the destination. Vale do Sol.

She smiled. They had made it.

They found seats near the middle. Lucas put his backpack on the floor. Mia placed her suitcase beside her. The bus began moving.

For the first half hour, they talked very little. Mia watched the city gradually disappear. Buildings became smaller. Then houses became less frequent. Fields appeared. The road curved between hills.

She had expected to feel nervous about being so far from the city. Instead, she felt something close to relief.

Lucas took photographs through the window. At one point, Mia asked, "What are you taking pictures of?"

"That tree."

She looked. "It looks normal."

"It does."

"Then why photograph it?"

Lucas lowered the camera. "Because it won't always be there."

Mia looked at the tree again. It was old and twisted, standing alone beside a stone wall. She understood. Or at least she thought she did.

"Do you take pictures of everything?"

"No."

"What do you choose?"

"Things I don't want to forget."

Mia smiled. She remembered her own notebook.

"That's what I write down."

Lucas looked at her. "You keep a notebook?"

"Yes."

"What do you write?"

"Things I notice."

He nodded. "Same idea."

She smiled. "Maybe."

The bus continued along the road. At some point, Mia fell asleep. When she woke, the landscape had changed again. The hills were greener. Small houses appeared in the distance.

Lucas was looking out the window. "We're close."

Mia sat up. She looked outside.

The village was spread across the valley below them. Red roofs. Stone walls. A church tower. Fields stretching toward the hills.

It looked nothing like the photographs she had seen online. It was quieter. Smaller. More ordinary. And somehow more beautiful.

When they got off the bus, the driver pointed toward the center of the village.

"Five minutes."

Mia thanked him.

They stood beside the road. Lucas looked around.

"Which way is your guesthouse?"

Mia checked her phone. "That way."

They started walking.

The village was almost silent. A dog barked somewhere behind a wall. A bicycle leaned against a doorway. An old woman watered flowers outside her house.

Mia slowed down. She wanted to remember everything.

They reached a small square. There was a fountain in the middle and a café on one side.

Mia checked the address again. "This is it."

Lucas looked at the guesthouse. "I think mine is further up."

They stood there. For the first time since leaving the station, Mia realized they were about to go separate ways.

It was strange how quickly a stranger could become familiar when you shared a canceled train, a walk, and a bus ride through the countryside.

"Thank you," she said.

"For what?"

"Helping me figure this out."

"You would have."

"Eventually."

He smiled. "Probably."

Mia picked up her suitcase. "Maybe I'll see you around."

"Maybe."

She started walking toward the guesthouse. Then Lucas called her name.

She turned.

"Your notebook."

Mia looked down. It was sticking out of the side pocket of her backpack.

She laughed. "Right."

Lucas smiled. "You don't want to lose that."

"No."

She waved. Then continued walking.

The guesthouse was smaller than she expected. A wooden sign hung above the entrance, and flowers grew along the stone wall.

Mia pushed open the door. A woman behind the reception desk looked up.

"Hello."

Mia gave her name. The woman checked a notebook. Then her expression changed.

"I'm sorry."

Mia felt a familiar tension return to her shoulders.

"Sorry?"

"There is a problem."

"What kind of problem?"

The woman looked embarrassed. "We have your reservation."

Mia waited.

"But we don't have your room."

For a moment, Mia simply stared at her. She looked at the woman. Then at the suitcase. Then back at the woman.

"You don't have my room?"

The woman shook her head. "There was a mistake."

Mia closed her eyes.

Of course. The train had been canceled. The bus had been complicated. And now the room didn't exist.

She took a slow breath. "Okay."

The woman began explaining, but Mia barely heard her. She looked through the window.

Outside, the village was calm. People walked slowly through the square. The fountain continued running. A bicycle passed. Somewhere nearby, someone was laughing.

Mia almost laughed too. Not because it was funny. Because it wasn't.

She had traveled thousands of kilometers to leave her carefully organized life behind. And somehow, her carefully organized life had followed her all the way there.

The woman behind the desk was still apologizing. Mia listened this time.

"We have another guesthouse."

"Where?"

"About fifteen minutes from here."

"Walking?"

The woman hesitated. "With your suitcase?"

Mia looked at her suitcase. Then out at the village.

She smiled. "Why not?"

The woman looked surprised.

Mia picked up the handle. "Let's go."

Outside, the afternoon sun had begun to soften.

Mia started walking.

She didn't know where she would sleep that night. She didn't know whether the other guesthouse would be comfortable. She didn't know what the next day would look like.

But she knew something else now.

A canceled train had brought her to a road she hadn't planned to take. A stranger had walked beside her. A bus had carried her through a landscape she had never seen. And now a missing hotel room was sending her somewhere else.

Perhaps this was what traveling really meant.

Not following the road you had planned.

But learning to keep walking when the road changed.

chapters.title: A Table for Two
chapters.content:
The second guesthouse was farther away than fifteen minutes.

Mia discovered this approximately twenty minutes after leaving the first one.

She didn't mind.

The road followed the edge of the village, passing stone houses with wooden shutters, gardens filled with herbs and flowers, and small walls covered in moss. There were no sidewalks for most of the way, so she had to pull her suitcase carefully along the uneven road while keeping an eye on the occasional car.

The guesthouse owner had given her simple directions.

"Follow the road until you see the old fountain. Then turn left."

Mia had nodded confidently.

Five minutes later, she realized there were three fountains.

She stopped.

For a moment, she considered taking out her phone.

Then she remembered Teresa.

If you know where you are going, you will only see what you expected.

Mia looked around.

She chose the fountain closest to a large olive tree.

It turned out to be the right one.

The guesthouse appeared at the end of a narrow lane.

It was a small white house with blue shutters and a wooden door covered in scratches. A few chairs stood outside beneath a vine-covered terrace.

An older man came out to greet her.

"You are Mia?"

"Yes."

He smiled.

"Come in."

Mia followed him inside.

The guesthouse was simple but beautiful. There were only six rooms, a small reception area, and a dining room with wooden tables. The walls were decorated with old photographs of the village, many of them black and white.

The man took her suitcase upstairs.

"I'm sorry about the mistake at the other place," he said.

"It's okay."

"It happens."

Mia smiled.

"Apparently, I'm getting used to things happening."

The man laughed.

"Good. That is useful here."

Her room overlooked the valley.

Mia stood by the window for several minutes without moving.

The sun was beginning to set behind the hills, turning the rooftops below a soft orange.

She opened the window.

The air smelled of grass and wood smoke.

For a moment, she forgot that she was supposed to be tired.

She unpacked only enough to find clean clothes.

Then she went downstairs.

The older man was sitting at a table.

"My name is António," he said.

"Mia."

"I know."

She smiled.

"Right."

He pointed toward another chair.

"Sit."

Mia sat.

"Do you serve dinner?"

António laughed.

"No."

"Oh."

"But my wife does."

He pointed toward the kitchen.

A woman's voice came from inside.

"Don't tell her that."

António laughed.

Mia smiled.

"You have a restaurant?"

"No. We have dinner."

She wasn't sure what that meant.

António stood.

"My wife is making too much food."

Mia immediately understood.

"You don't have to."

"We know."

He walked toward the kitchen.

Mia sat alone for a moment.

Then she heard his wife say something in Portuguese.

António answered.

They began talking.

Mia couldn't understand the words, but she understood the tone.

There was something warm about the exchange.

Something familiar.

A few minutes later, a woman came out carrying a bowl.

She was perhaps in her late sixties, with gray hair tied behind her head.

"This is my wife, Rosa."

Rosa smiled.

"Mia."

"Hello."

"Dinner."

Mia stood.

"I'd be happy to pay."

Rosa waved her hand.

"No."

"Really, I can."

"No."

She placed the bowl on the table.

"You are traveling alone."

Mia nodded.

"So tonight you are not eating alone."

Mia looked at her.

Something in the simplicity of the sentence caught her off guard.

"Thank you."

Rosa smiled.

"Sit."

So Mia did.

Dinner was simple.

Soup.

Bread.

Roasted vegetables.

Rice.

A plate of fish.

Nothing looked like the carefully photographed meals in travel magazines. There were no decorative arrangements or complicated sauces. Everything was served in large dishes in the middle of the table.

Mia liked it immediately.

António poured wine into three glasses.

Mia raised her hand.

"I don't usually drink much."

Rosa looked at her.

"Then drink little."

Mia laughed.

"Fair."

They ate.

At first, conversation was difficult.

Mia knew very little Portuguese, and António and Rosa knew only a few words of English.

They found ways around it.

Mia pointed.

They explained.

They laughed when they misunderstood each other.

Eventually, the conversation became easier.

Rosa asked about Mia's family.

Mia told her about her parents.

António asked about her work.

"Travel agency."

He looked surprised.

"You travel a lot?"

Mia smiled.

"Other people do."

Rosa laughed.

António understood.

"Ah."

Mia shook her head.

"No, really. I plan trips for people."

"And this is your first?"

"Alone."

António nodded slowly.

"Why?"

Mia looked down at her plate.

She could have given him a simple answer.

Vacation.

Curiosity.

A friend's ticket.

Instead, she told the truth.

"I think I needed to go somewhere I didn't know."

Rosa watched her.

"Because?"

Mia hesitated.

"Because I know my life too well."

António smiled.

Rosa looked at him.

They exchanged a few words.

Then Rosa turned to Mia.

"Sometimes knowing too much is also a problem."

Mia smiled.

"I think I'm learning that."

After dinner, António brought out a small bottle of something he called local.

Mia took a very small sip.

Her eyes widened.

Rosa laughed.

"Too strong?"

"Very."

They laughed together.

Later, Mia stood outside beneath the terrace.

The village was almost completely dark.

There were only a few lights visible in the distance.

She could hear insects in the grass and the faint sound of voices from somewhere down the road.

She realized she had not checked her phone for almost two hours.

That alone felt unusual.

She took it from her pocket.

There were messages from Claire and her mother.

She answered both.

Then another message appeared.

From Lucas.

Lucas: Did you find a place to stay?

Mia smiled.

Mia: Eventually.

Lucas: Good.

Mia: They gave my room away.

Lucas: That's unfortunate.

Mia: I ended up at a guesthouse.

Lucas: Is it terrible?

Mia looked around.

The lights beneath the terrace.

The dark hills.

The quiet road.

She smiled.

Mia: No. It's actually beautiful.

A few seconds later:

Lucas: Then maybe the mistake was useful.

Mia looked at the message.

Mia: Maybe.

She put the phone away.

The next morning, Mia woke to the sound of birds.

For several seconds, she didn't know where she was.

Then she remembered.

Portugal.

The village.

The canceled train.

The missing room.

She smiled.

She dressed and went downstairs.

Breakfast was already waiting.

Rosa had placed bread, fruit, cheese, coffee, and eggs on the table.

"Good morning."

"Good morning."

Mia sat down.

Rosa joined her.

"Sleep well?"

"Very."

Rosa smiled.

"You are staying another night."

It wasn't a question.

Mia laughed.

"I hadn't planned to."

"Plans."

Rosa shook her head.

"They make people tired."

Mia smiled.

She understood.

After breakfast, she walked through the village.

She found a small market, a church, and a path leading toward the hills.

She walked for hours.

At first, she took photographs.

Then she stopped.

She wanted to remember things without turning everything into an image.

A man repairing a wooden door.

A woman hanging clothes from a balcony.

Children running through a square.

A cat sleeping beneath a car.

A bicycle with flowers in its basket.

The smell of bread coming from a bakery.

The sound of someone playing a guitar behind an open window.

None of these things were famous.

None would appear on a list of the ten best places to visit in the country.

But Mia began to understand that a place wasn't made important by how many people had photographed it.

It became important because someone had lived there.

Someone had cooked there.

Someone had waited there.

Someone had fallen in love there.

Someone had grown old there.

She stopped beside an old stone wall.

Her notebook was in her backpack.

She took it out.

She wrote:

Today I realized that being somewhere is different from seeing somewhere.

She read the sentence.

Then added:

I think I've spent a lot of time seeing.

She closed the notebook.

When she returned to the guesthouse in the afternoon, Lucas was sitting on the terrace.

Mia stopped.

He looked up.

"Hi."

She smiled.

"Hi."

"What are you doing here?"

"Apparently, my guesthouse is this one."

Mia laughed.

"Apparently."

Lucas pointed toward the chair beside him.

"Sit."

She sat.

He had his camera on the table.

"You found me."

"I wasn't looking."

"Neither was I."

They smiled.

For a while, they watched the village.

Then Lucas said, "How was your morning?"

"Good."

"Where did you go?"

"Everywhere."

He smiled.

"That's not an answer."

"It's the best one I have."

Lucas laughed.

Mia looked at his camera.

"Did you take many photographs?"

"Some."

"Can I see?"

He hesitated.

Then turned the camera toward her.

There were photographs of the village.

The old tree.

A house with blue shutters.

A woman carrying groceries.

A dog sleeping near a doorway.

The fountain.

The road they had walked together.

Mia stopped at one photograph.

It showed the village from above.

The hills stretched into the distance.

A narrow road disappeared around a bend.

"That's beautiful."

Lucas nodded.

"I took it this morning."

"Why?"

"Because I liked the road."

Mia looked at him.

"Where does it go?"

"I don't know."

She smiled.

"Of course you don't."

Lucas turned the camera off.

"You like knowing where roads go?"

"I used to."

"And now?"

Mia looked toward the road.

"I'm not sure."

They sat in silence.

It wasn't uncomfortable.

A few minutes later, Rosa came outside.

She looked at them.

Then at the empty table.

Then back at them.

"Dinner."

Lucas smiled.

"Thank you."

Rosa looked at Mia.

"You have a table."

Mia glanced at Lucas.

Then at Rosa.

"Together?"

Rosa nodded.

"Of course."

She walked back inside.

Mia laughed softly.

Lucas looked at her.

"Well."

"Well."

They followed Rosa into the dining room.

That evening, there were only two plates on the table.

Mia looked at them.

"Looks like we're sharing dinner."

Lucas smiled.

"Looks like it."

Outside, the village grew quiet.

Inside, two strangers sat at a small wooden table, eating food prepared by people who had met them only the day before.

They talked about places they had been, places they wanted to see, books, photographs, families, and the strange feeling of being somewhere unfamiliar.

Mia told Lucas about the travel agency. He told her about his photography project.

Neither of them told the other everything.

There was no need.

Some stories needed time.

After dinner, they stayed at the table long after the plates had been cleared.

Mia realized she wasn't thinking about when she would leave. She wasn't thinking about her itinerary. She wasn't thinking about work. She wasn't thinking about what she would do when she returned home.

She was simply there.

At a table.

In a village she hadn't planned to visit.

Beside someone she had met because a train had been canceled.

And for the first time since beginning the journey, Mia understood that perhaps the best parts of traveling were not the places you carefully chose.

They were the moments that had no reason to happen at all.

chapters.title: The Things We Carry
chapters.content:
The next morning, Mia woke before the alarm she had forgotten to set.

For a few seconds, she lay still beneath the thin white blanket, listening to the sounds coming from outside her window. Somewhere below, a door opened and closed. A car started in the distance, followed by the low bark of a dog. Someone was speaking loudly enough that she could hear the rhythm of the conversation without understanding a single word.

She turned toward the window.

The sky was pale blue, and the first light of morning rested on the rooftops across the valley.

At home, mornings had always arrived differently. Her alarm would ring at exactly seven. She would reach for her phone before she was fully awake, check the time, glance at her messages, and then begin moving through the sequence of actions she had repeated so many times that she no longer needed to think about them. Shower. Clothes. Coffee. Train. Work.

Here, there was no sequence.

There was only morning.

Mia got dressed and went downstairs.

Rosa was already in the kitchen.

"You are early," she said.

"I couldn't sleep anymore."

Rosa placed a cup of coffee on the table.

"That is because you are thinking."

Mia smiled.

"I do that sometimes."

"Sometimes?"

Mia laughed.

Rosa sat across from her.

"You think too much."

"I know."

"About what?"

Mia looked at the coffee.

"Everything."

Rosa nodded as though that were a perfectly understandable answer.

"Then eat."

Mia smiled.

Breakfast was quieter than the night before. There was something comfortable about that. She didn't need to fill every silence with conversation, and Rosa seemed equally comfortable allowing the morning to happen around them.

When Mia finished, she went upstairs and began packing.

This time, she did it differently.

At home, she had always packed carefully. Everything folded into its place, shoes separated from clothes, toiletries arranged inside small bags, cables wrapped and secured. She liked knowing where everything was.

Now she stood in the middle of the room with a sweater in her hands and wondered whether she really needed it.

She looked at the suitcase.

Then at the sweater.

Then back at the suitcase.

"You're not helping," she said aloud.

There was no one there to answer.

She put the sweater inside anyway.

When she came downstairs, Lucas was sitting outside with a cup of coffee.

His camera was beside him.

"You look ready to leave," he said.

"I am."

"Where are you going?"

"I don't know yet."

Lucas smiled.

"That's progress."

Mia sat across from him.

"You say that like it's easy."

"It isn't."

"Then why do you do it?"

He looked toward the road.

"Because I've spent a lot of time doing the opposite."

Mia waited.

Lucas didn't immediately explain.

Instead, he picked up his camera and checked something on the screen.

Eventually, he said, "I used to have everything planned."

"Everything?"

"Not literally everything."

"Just most things?"

He smiled.

"Most important things."

Mia understood that distinction.

"What changed?"

Lucas leaned back in his chair.

"My father died."

The sentence came quietly.

Not dramatically.

Not as if he expected sympathy.

Mia didn't know what to say.

"I'm sorry."

Lucas nodded.

"It was a few years ago."

He looked at the camera.

"He was the kind of person who had a plan for everything. Work. Money. Holidays. Retirement. Even what he wanted to do with the garden when he was seventy."

Mia smiled faintly.

"Sounds familiar."

"Very."

Lucas was quiet for a moment.

"After he died, I realized I had spent years waiting for the future he had described."

Mia looked at him.

"What do you mean?"

"I thought I would eventually have time. Time to travel. Time to take photographs. Time to do things that didn't have a practical purpose."

He looked toward the hills.

"Then one day I understood that 'later' isn't a place you can actually reach."

Mia lowered her eyes.

She had heard something similar before.

Not from Lucas.

From Teresa.

From herself.

Maybe from everyone she had been avoiding listening to.

"What did you do?" she asked.

"I quit my job."

Mia looked at him.

"You just quit?"

"Not immediately."

"Good."

He laughed.

"No. I thought about it for almost a year."

"That sounds more like it."

"I saved some money. Sold my apartment. Kept what I needed. Then I started traveling."

"And you've been doing that ever since?"

"Mostly."

Mia looked at his camera.

"Is that why you take photographs?"

Lucas nodded.

"My father used to write things down."

Mia's expression changed.

"Really?"

"Everything. Places he'd been. Things people said. Little things."

He smiled.

"After he died, I found notebooks everywhere."

Mia remembered the small black notebook she had seen him carrying on the train.

"You write too?"

"Sometimes."

"What do you write?"

"Things I don't want to forget."

Mia smiled.

"I have one of those."

Lucas looked at her.

"I know."

She touched the notebook inside her bag.

"Claire gave it to me."

"Who's Claire?"

"My friend."

"The one who gave you the ticket?"

"Yes."

Lucas nodded.

"What did you write in it?"

Mia thought about the first page.

"The first day?"

"Yes."

"I wrote that I thought traveling would feel bigger."

Lucas waited.

"And?"

"I think I was wrong."

He smiled.

"That's usually how travel works."

Mia laughed.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

Then Lucas pointed toward her suitcase.

"What's in there?"

Mia looked at him.

"Clothes."

"I know that."

"Books."

"How many?"

"Two."

"That's too many."

"They're small."

"Still."

She smiled.

"Why are you interrogating my luggage?"

"I'm curious."

Mia thought about it.

"Probably too much."

"Everyone brings too much."

"Do you?"

Lucas glanced toward his backpack.

"Of course."

"What's the heaviest thing?"

He considered the question.

"Probably the camera."

"That's physical."

"I know."

Mia smiled.

"I meant something else."

Lucas looked at her.

She realized she had asked a question she hadn't intended to ask.

But he didn't avoid it.

"My expectations," he said.

Mia didn't answer.

Neither did he.

The words seemed to remain between them for a while.

Eventually, Mia looked toward her own suitcase.

"I think I brought mine too."

"What expectations?"

"That this trip would tell me what to do with my life."

Lucas smiled gently.

"That's a lot to ask from a trip."

"I know."

"Did you at least ask for a refund?"

She laughed.

"Not yet."

They left the guesthouse late that morning.

Mia had planned to continue north.

Lucas was heading toward the coast.

Neither of them had originally intended to travel together.

It simply happened.

They walked through the village toward a small bus station.

Mia carried her suitcase.

Lucas carried his backpack and camera.

At the station, there was a handwritten timetable taped to the wall.

Lucas studied it.

"There is a bus in forty minutes."

"Where does it go?"

"Toward the coast."

Mia looked at him.

"How far?"

"About two hours."

"Where exactly?"

He pointed at the timetable.

"Somewhere around here."

She laughed.

"That's not a destination."

"It is if we get off."

Mia looked at the road.

Then at the timetable.

Then at her suitcase.

For years, she had believed that a good trip required a destination.

A reservation.

A schedule.

A return ticket.

Now she was standing beside a man who seemed perfectly comfortable with the idea of getting off a bus somewhere neither of them had ever been.

"Fine," she said.

Lucas smiled.

"Fine?"

"Let's do it."

The bus arrived forty minutes later.

They climbed aboard and found two seats near the back.

The village disappeared behind them.

The road climbed through the hills before beginning a long descent toward the sea.

Mia watched the landscape through the window.

Fields became forests.

Forests became open hills.

Then, suddenly, the ocean appeared.

She leaned closer to the glass.

It stretched across the horizon, bright beneath the afternoon sun.

She had seen oceans before.

She had photographs of them.

She had stood beside them on family vacations.

But this one felt different.

Perhaps because she hadn't planned to see it today.

She took out her notebook.

Lucas noticed.

"What are you writing?"

She shook her head.

"Nothing yet."

"Why?"

"I don't know what to say."

"That's usually when something is worth writing about."

Mia smiled.

She opened the notebook.

Then wrote:

Today we took a bus without knowing exactly where it would take us.

She stopped.

Then added:

I thought that would make me nervous.

She looked out at the sea.

It doesn't.

She closed the notebook.

Lucas didn't ask to read it.

Mia appreciated that.

The bus continued along the coast.

They passed beaches hidden between cliffs, small houses with red roofs, fishing boats resting in narrow harbors, and roads that seemed to disappear into the hills.

Eventually, Lucas leaned forward.

"There's a town coming up."

Mia looked at him.

"Do we get off?"

He smiled.

"Do you want to?"

Mia looked out the window.

The town appeared in the distance.

She thought about her suitcase.

Her job.

Her apartment.

Her parents.

The life waiting for her.

Then she thought about the road ahead.

"I don't know," she said.

Lucas nodded.

"Good answer."

When the bus stopped, neither of them moved immediately.

People got off.

Others climbed aboard.

The driver waited.

Mia looked at Lucas.

He looked at her.

Then she stood.

"Let's go."

They stepped off the bus.

The doors closed behind them.

The bus disappeared down the road.

Mia watched it until it turned around a bend.

For a moment, she felt something she couldn't quite name.

It wasn't fear.

It wasn't excitement.

It was the strange sensation of having closed one door without knowing what would open next.

She picked up her suitcase.

Lucas lifted his backpack.

Ahead of them was a narrow street leading toward the sea.

There was no reservation.

No carefully chosen hotel.

No list of things they needed to see.

Just a road.

Mia smiled.

For once, that was enough.

chapters.title: The Long Way to the Sea
chapters.content:
The town was smaller than Mia had expected.

There was one main street, a row of white buildings with faded shutters, a bakery that seemed to be doing most of its business before noon, and a small square where several elderly men sat beneath the shade of a tree, watching the world move past them. The sea was somewhere beyond the houses, close enough that Mia could smell salt in the air, but the streets twisted in ways that made it difficult to tell which direction they were actually going.

She stood beside her suitcase and looked at Lucas.

"So where are we?"

He took out his phone, looked at the screen, and then put it away.

Mia raised an eyebrow.

"You don't know?"

"I know the name of the town."

"That's reassuring."

"I didn't say I knew anything else."

She laughed.

They started walking.

There was something strangely pleasant about not knowing where they were going. Mia had expected uncertainty to feel like a weight, something she would have to constantly resist. Instead, it seemed lighter than certainty had ever felt.

They stopped at the bakery because Lucas said he was hungry.

Mia wasn't particularly hungry, but she ordered something anyway.

They sat outside with coffee and pastries while the town moved around them. A woman carried two bags of groceries across the street. A boy rode a bicycle too quickly around the square and was immediately shouted at by an older man. A dog wandered beneath their table, looked up at Mia as if expecting to be fed, and then moved on when she offered nothing.

Lucas watched the street through his camera.

"You photograph everything," Mia said.

"Not everything."

"Almost everything."

He lowered the camera.

"Only the things I notice."

"What makes you notice something?"

"I don't know."

"You really don't know?"

He thought about it.

"Sometimes it's because something is beautiful. Sometimes because it's disappearing. Sometimes because someone looks happy. Sometimes because they don't."

Mia looked at him.

"And sometimes?"

"Sometimes I just want to remember where I was."

She nodded.

That answer made sense to her.

After breakfast, they found a small car rental office at the edge of town.

The woman behind the desk spoke very little English, but after a combination of gestures, photographs, and Lucas's limited Portuguese, they managed to rent an old blue car for two days.

Mia stared at it.

"You trust this thing?"

Lucas opened the driver's door.

"It has four wheels."

"That's not a guarantee."

He laughed.

She put her suitcase in the trunk.

There was barely enough room.

"Perfect," she said.

Lucas looked at her.

"You've changed."

"What?"

"You would have measured the trunk before agreeing to this."

Mia smiled.

"Maybe."

They drove toward the coast.

At first, Lucas followed the main road.

Then they passed a sign pointing toward a smaller road.

He slowed down.

Mia looked at the sign.

"What does that say?"

Lucas translated.

"Beach."

"Is it the beach?"

"Probably."

"Probably?"

"That's what the sign says."

Mia smiled.

"Turn."

He turned.

The road narrowed almost immediately.

The pavement became rough.

Trees grew close to both sides.

After several minutes, the road opened onto a small clearing.

Beyond it was the ocean.

Mia got out of the car before Lucas had even turned off the engine.

She walked toward the edge of the cliff.

The sea stretched endlessly below.

There was a narrow beach far beneath them, almost completely empty.

Lucas came to stand beside her.

Neither spoke.

The wind moved through Mia's hair.

She closed her eyes for a moment.

She thought about the office.

The train.

The calendar on her desk.

The stack of documents waiting for her.

The apartment she had left behind.

All of it suddenly seemed very far away.

"Beautiful," she said.

Lucas nodded.

"Yes."

Mia looked at him.

"Do you ever get tired of seeing places like this?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I'm never the same person twice."

She looked back toward the ocean.

"What does that mean?"

"Every time I return somewhere, I'm different. So the place is different too."

Mia thought about that.

Maybe that was why familiar places sometimes felt strange after long periods away.

Maybe places didn't stay still.

Maybe people didn't either.

They spent the afternoon driving along the coast.

Sometimes they stopped because there was a view.

Sometimes because there was a small café.

Once because Lucas saw a group of fishing boats and wanted to photograph them.

Another time because Mia noticed a field of wildflowers and insisted on stopping.

They ate sandwiches sitting on a low stone wall overlooking the water.

They talked about small things.

Mia told him about a book she had read years ago and still remembered.

Lucas told her about the first photograph he had ever taken seriously.

She asked about his family.

He asked about hers.

The conversation moved easily between subjects, never staying too long in one place.

At one point, they passed a sign pointing toward a village.

Mia read it aloud.

"São Miguel."

Lucas slowed down.

"Do you want to go?"

Mia looked at him.

"Is there anything there?"

"Probably."

She laughed.

"You're becoming a problem."

"Why?"

"You've started using my least favorite word."

"Probably?"

"Exactly."

They turned.

The village was only a few minutes away.

It was smaller than the town they had left.

There was a church, a small grocery store, several houses, and a café with three tables outside.

A man was sweeping the pavement.

A woman was watering flowers.

A child was drawing with chalk near the church steps.

Mia felt strangely calm.

She had spent most of her adult life believing that a day needed a purpose.

This day didn't.

It simply happened.

They walked through the village.

Lucas took photographs.

Mia watched.

At the edge of the village, they found a path leading toward the water.

It wasn't marked on any map they had.

They followed it.

The path descended between rocks and bushes until the trees opened.

Below them was a small cove.

The beach was empty.

Mia took off her shoes.

Lucas looked at her.

"What are you doing?"

"Walking."

"Without shoes?"

"Yes."

He smiled.

She stepped onto the sand.

It was warm beneath her feet.

The tide had left small pools between the rocks, reflecting the sky.

Lucas stayed behind for a moment.

Then he took off his shoes too.

They walked along the shoreline.

Mia rolled up the bottom of her trousers when the water reached her ankles.

Lucas took a photograph.

She turned.

"Did you just take a picture of me?"

"Yes."

"Without asking?"

He lowered the camera.

"Sorry."

Mia looked at him.

She expected to be annoyed.

Instead, she smiled.

"It's okay."

He raised the camera again.

"Are you sure?"

She nodded.

This time, she didn't look at the camera.

She looked toward the sea.

The shutter clicked.

Then again.

Mia continued walking.

She didn't ask to see the photograph.

She didn't need to.

Later, they sat on the sand.

The sun was beginning to lower.

Lucas rested his arms on his knees.

"You know," he said, "most people would probably have spent today somewhere else."

"Where?"

"Somewhere they planned to be."

Mia smiled.

"I was supposed to be somewhere else too."

"Where?"

"I don't remember."

Lucas laughed.

"That's progress."

She looked at him.

"Do you ever worry that you're wasting time?"

"All the time."

Mia was surprised.

"Really?"

"Of course."

"What do you do about it?"

"I keep going."

She considered that.

"That's it?"

"Sometimes."

"And the other times?"

"I go home."

Mia looked toward the horizon.

"Do you have a home?"

Lucas was quiet.

"Not really."

The answer surprised her.

She didn't ask another question.

After a while, he said, "Maybe that's what I'm looking for."

"A home?"

"Maybe."

Mia smiled.

"You're not very good at knowing what you're looking for."

"No."

She looked at him.

"Neither am I."

They stayed on the beach until the light began to fade.

Eventually, they returned to the car.

They found a small guesthouse in the village and asked for two rooms.

There was only one available.

Mia looked at Lucas.

The owner was already apologizing.

"One room."

Mia smiled.

"Two beds?"

The woman nodded.

Lucas looked at Mia.

"If you're uncomfortable—"

"It's fine."

The room was simple.

Two separate beds.

One small window.

A wooden wardrobe.

A table with a lamp.

There was nothing romantic about it.

And Mia was grateful for that.

They were two people traveling through a country neither had planned to explore together.

For now, that was enough.

After showering, Mia went outside.

The village was quiet.

There were lights in the windows of the houses.

Someone was cooking nearby.

She sat on a low wall and opened her notebook.

She wrote for a long time.

Not about the places.

Not about the sea.

Not even about Lucas.

She wrote about herself.

About how strange it felt to wake up without knowing what the day would demand from her.

About how she had always confused control with safety.

About how many decisions she had postponed because she was waiting to become the kind of person who knew exactly what she wanted.

She stopped writing.

Then added one final sentence.

Maybe you don't have to know where you are going to start moving.

She closed the notebook.

Lucas came outside.

"You disappeared."

"I was here."

"I know."

He sat beside her.

For a while, they watched the dark street.

Then Lucas said, "Tomorrow, I want to go farther north."

Mia looked at him.

"How far?"

"Until the road ends."

She smiled.

"That's not a real plan."

"I know."

She looked toward the darkness beyond the houses.

Then back at him.

"Okay."

"Okay?"

"Let's see where the road ends."

Lucas smiled.

Neither of them knew that the road ahead would not take them where they expected.

Neither knew that the car would eventually stop, that their carefully improvised journey would force them into a place neither had heard of, or that being stranded there would make Mia confront the one thing she had been avoiding since the beginning of the trip.

For now, there was only the sea beyond the village, the road waiting in the morning, and the quiet certainty that sometimes the longest way somewhere begins when you stop asking how long it will take.

chapters.title: A Place Without a Name
chapters.content:
The road seemed to have no intention of ending.

By late morning, Mia had stopped asking where they were going. The blue car moved along the coast, sometimes close enough to the water that she could see the waves breaking against the rocks below, sometimes disappearing inland through fields and small forests. The road narrowed and widened without warning, and every few miles they passed another sign pointing toward a village, a beach, or a place whose name Mia had never heard before.

She sat with her elbow against the window, watching the landscape change.

There was something different about the coast in the morning. The light was clearer, almost silver, and the sea seemed less like scenery and more like something alive beside them. Fishing boats appeared and disappeared in the distance. Small houses stood alone among fields. Laundry moved on lines between buildings, bright against white walls.

Lucas drove with one hand resting casually on the steering wheel.

"You've been quiet," he said.

"I'm looking."

"At what?"

"Everything."

He smiled.

"That's a lot."

"I have a lot to catch up on."

He glanced at her.

She didn't explain.

There were some things Mia still couldn't put into words.

They continued for another hour before the car began making a strange noise.

At first, Mia ignored it.

Then it happened again.

A low metallic sound came from somewhere beneath them.

Lucas frowned.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"That sounded like something."

"I know."

The car continued.

A few minutes later, the engine lost power.

Lucas guided the car toward the side of the road.

The engine stopped.

Silence filled the car.

Mia looked at him.

"That doesn't sound good."

Lucas tried the ignition.

Nothing.

He tried again.

Still nothing.

Mia waited.

Then she laughed.

Lucas turned toward her.

"What?"

"We're stranded."

"Apparently."

She laughed again.

"I've never been stranded before."

"There's a first time for everything."

"Do you know how to fix a car?"

"No."

"Excellent."

Lucas smiled.

"I know how to call someone who does."

He took out his phone.

There was almost no signal.

He held it up.

Nothing.

Mia looked around.

They were on a narrow road surrounded by trees and fields.

There were no buildings nearby.

No other cars.

No signs.

No people.

"Where are we?"

Lucas looked at the road.

"I don't know."

Mia laughed.

"Of course you don't."

He looked at the phone again.

"There's a village a few kilometers away."

"How do you know?"

"There was a sign."

"I didn't see it."

"You were looking at the ocean."

She smiled.

"Fair."

They took what they needed from the car.

Mia carried her backpack.

Lucas carried his camera.

They locked the car and began walking.

The road curved around a hill.

For the first few minutes, neither spoke.

Then Mia said, "Are you worried?"

"About what?"

"The car."

"No."

"Really?"

"Someone will eventually find it."

"And us?"

He looked at her.

"We're walking toward a village."

"You sound very confident."

"I've been lost before."

Mia smiled.

"I haven't."

"You will be."

"That's comforting."

They walked for almost an hour.

The road gradually became narrower.

Eventually, they saw several houses in the distance.

The village was barely large enough to call itself one.

There were perhaps twenty houses, a small church, a grocery store, and a café with a faded sign above the door.

A woman was standing outside the grocery store.

She watched them approach.

Lucas greeted her.

They explained their situation with a mixture of Portuguese, English, gestures, and laughter.

The woman understood.

She pointed toward the café.

"Coffee."

Mia looked at Lucas.

"I think she just invited us for coffee."

"That sounds like a good idea."

The café was almost empty.

An older man sat near the window reading a newspaper.

Two women were talking quietly at a table.

The owner brought Mia and Lucas coffee without asking what they wanted.

Mia took a sip.

It was strong.

Very strong.

She looked at Lucas.

"Everyone here makes coffee like they have something against sleep."

He laughed.

The woman who had brought them inside sat down at their table.

Her name was Ana.

She was in her seventies and had lived in the village all her life.

She asked about the car.

Lucas explained.

Ana shook her head.

"Mechanic."

She pointed toward the road.

"Tomorrow."

Mia looked surprised.

"Tomorrow?"

Ana nodded.

"Today?"

She shrugged.

"No."

Lucas laughed.

Mia looked at him.

"So we're staying."

"Looks like it."

Ana smiled.

"Rooms."

She pointed toward the café.

"Upstairs."

Mia blinked.

"You have rooms?"

Ana nodded.

"Two."

She held up two fingers.

Mia smiled.

"Of course you do."

Ana laughed.

The rooms were above the café.

Small.

Clean.

Simple.

Mia had stopped being surprised by how quickly a problem could turn into a place to stay.

She left her bag upstairs and returned to the café.

Lucas was sitting outside.

Ana was talking to him.

They were laughing about something.

Mia sat down.

"What did I miss?"

"Apparently, Ana thinks you're too serious."

Mia looked at Ana.

"She doesn't even know me."

Ana pointed at her notebook.

"Always writing."

Mia smiled.

"She's not wrong."

Ana nodded as though she had proved her point.

The rest of the afternoon passed slowly.

There was nowhere they needed to be.

No train to catch.

No reservation waiting.

No itinerary.

Mia walked around the village.

She found an old stone fountain.

A small cemetery behind the church.

A field filled with yellow flowers.

A house with blue doors.
